```{r setup}
library(allocatR)
```

This vignette covers use of the allocatR package to randomly assign participants
in a randomised clinical trial. It assumes that R can be connected to your trial
infrastructure through one of the following:
* R is run directly on the server containing trial data
* R is run remotely using an API call to the server containing trial data
* Randomisation is fully self-contained within e.g. a locally run Shiny app for managing randomisation.

The specific method of integration is beyond the scope of this vignette and will
vary with your implementation. For illustrative purposes, this vignette uses code
compatible with the Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) API. 

## Data import



```{r}

# If randomisation script is called from a command line call using Rscript,
# the ID can be passed as an argument

# args = commandArgs(trailingOnly = TRUE)
# id <- args[1]

id <- "5"

```


```{r}
# Use REDCap's API to load data

library(REDCapR) # Load the package into the current R session.
uri   <- "https://redcap-dev-2.ouhsc.edu/redcap/api/"
token <- "9A068C425B1341D69E83064A2D273A70" # simple

read_data <- as.data.frame(redcap_read(redcap_uri = uri, token = token)$data)

# In a trial data set, the arm would be one of the columns read from above
read_data$arm <- c(0,1,0,1,NA)

# Structure the data how we need it to be structured
# We use BMI and read_data as examples.
read_data <- existing_data[,c("record_id","age","sex","bmi","ethnicity","arm")]
read_data$ethnicity <- factor(read_data$ethnicity, ordered=FALSE)
read_data$sex <- factor(read_data$sex, ordered=FALSE)


# The allocation function feeds in data separately for participants that have
# been randomised, and the participant to be randomised. We need to separate this out.

existing_data <- read_data[which(read_data$record_id != id),]
new_data <- read_data[which(read_data$record_id == id),]


```

Alternatively, data can be written to disk, by some other mechanism and then read
by R using e.g. read.csv()

Regardless of the method of reading data, the final step prior to randomisation
is to perform checks of data quality. If randomisation requires data have to
complete data (all current methods need complete data), missing data in
existing data will break randomisation. The easiest fix for this is to simply allocate
imbalance based on complete case current data.

**NOTE** this workflow means that record deletion (or participants who lose these baseline variables
later) may lead to re-use of the random sequence. To account for this, use the optional offset
argument in allocate() to jump the sequence ahead by some number of allocations.

```{r}

# Run randomisation only using those people with complete data (i.e. treatment assigned and all relevant covariates observed)

has_missing <- do.call("c",
        sapply(1:ncol(existing_data),function(i){which(is.na(existing_data[,i]))})
)

if(length(has_missing)>0){
  existing_data[-has_missing,]
}

```

Also check for anything that looks wrong about the data, and error if we're missing
data on the new person

```{r}

if(!is.na(new_data$arm)) stop(sprintf("ID %s is already randomised",id))

for(i in c("age","sex","bmi","ethnicity")){
  if(is.na(new_data[,i])) stop(sprintf("ID %s is missing a value for %s",id,i))
}

```
